title: Redlands Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Redlands wells have a 22-foot median depth, but records range to 1,690 feet. See yield, water levels, risks and local drilling costs.
h1: Redlands, Colorado Well Depth, Yield and Cost Guide
intro_html:
Well conditions in Redlands vary sharply by location and by the kind of well being counted. Within five miles of Redlands, Colorado DWR records include 1,025 permitted wells, but only 378 are recorded as constructed. Many records are monitoring wells rather than household-supply wells, so the local numbers are useful for planning but not a substitute for a site-specific evaluation.

The area includes Grand Junction, Fruita, Orchard Mesa, Glade Park, Fruitvale and Clifton. Before buying land or starting a build, compare nearby well permits, confirm the intended use with Colorado DWR, and have a driller evaluate access, geology, casing, grout, pump equipment and septic layout.

sections.heading: Redlands well depth depends on the ground below the lot
sections.html:
The recorded median well depth near Redlands is 22 feet, with the middle half between 16 and 40 feet. That shallow result is strongly influenced by the local record set, which includes many monitoring wells. The range is still substantial: the 90th-percentile depth is 394 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 1,690 feet.

Most reported wells, 79%, are under 100 feet. Another 7% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 8% between 300 and 600 feet, and 6% exceed 600 feet. A driller should not price a Redlands home-site well from the median alone. Ask for a bid with a depth allowance and a clear per-foot rate if the hole must go deeper.

sections.heading: What Redlands wells produce for household use
sections.html:
Among the 56 records reporting pump yield, the median is 12.2 gallons per minute. The middle half runs from 7.9 to 15.0 gallons per minute, which is generally a workable production range for ordinary household demand when the well, pressure system and storage are properly designed.

Yield records are uneven: 54% report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 45% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Only 2% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, and none are recorded under 1 gallon per minute. That does not guarantee a strong well on a particular parcel. A pump test, well-completion report and intended use matter more than the area median.

sections.heading: Redlands water levels do not show a simple falling trend
sections.html:
The recorded median static water level is 12 feet below the surface, with the middle half between 8 and 19 feet. These measurements describe the water level when a well is not being pumped, not the total depth of the well and not necessarily the level during a dry season.

By measurement decade, the median was 17 feet in the 2000s, 10 feet in the 2010s and 12 feet in the 2020s. That series does not establish a steadily dropping water table; the later median is shallower than the 2000s figure. Conditions can still differ by aquifer, irrigation activity, season and well location, so check the original measurement date and nearby records before relying on a water-level comparison.

sections.heading: Redlands permit history shows long, varied drilling activity
sections.html:
Permits in the Redlands area go back to the 1950s, and the newest permit year in the records is 2025. Issuance was highest in the 2000s, with 274 permits, followed by 240 in the 2010s and 176 in the 2020s. The record also includes 123 permits from the 1990s, 42 from the 1980s, 19 from the 1950s, 15 from the 1970s and 9 from the 1960s.

The most active named record entry is Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 341 records. Owner entries account for 17, and Artesian Services Inc. (Himes, Brad) appears on 12. A permit name is not a guarantee of current availability or workmanship. Confirm licensing, references, scope and who will perform the work before hiring.

sections.heading: Local Redlands well drilling cost starts with depth and completion
sections.html:
For the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground reported around Redlands, the drilling model uses a typical rate of $50 to $75 per foot. At the local median depth, the drilled hole alone works out to about $1,100 to $1,600. That is not the finished project price.

A completed well with pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $7,100 to $13,600 at the median depth. Deeper drilling, difficult access, casing and grout requirements, an upgraded electrical run or unusual pump equipment can change the bid. Have the contractor separate drilling, casing, grout, pump, tank, trenching, electrical and testing so competing estimates can be compared properly.

sections.heading: Redlands buyers need to check water quality, yield and septic layout
sections.html:
Permit records name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer for 864 wells, Alluvial for 37, and Entrada for 10. Fractured-rock production can be unpredictable because water may depend on individual fractures rather than a uniform layer. The records identify no Denver Basin aquifer wells, but that does not remove the need to verify the actual well and its legal use.

Environmental screening also deserves attention. Within about ten miles, the mapped information includes 69 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1 historic mine feature and 13 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test existing well water and review nearby site information. Keep the well, septic system and building area separated as required, and confirm that the lot has enough room for replacement or repair access.

sections.heading: How to evaluate a Redlands lot before building
sections.html:
Start with the well permit number, completion report, measured depth, pump yield, static water level and permitted use. Only 68 records report a static water level and 56 report a pump yield, so missing data is common. A domestic or household permit is different from a monitoring permit, and the local use mix is 66% monitoring, 10% domestic or household, 4% irrigation and 1% stock.

For a purchase, ask for a recent flow and water-quality test, service history, electrical details and proof that the well can serve the proposed home. For a new build, have a licensed driller and septic designer review the site together. Colorado DWR rules control the permit and use. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be necessary, so resolve water-rights questions before closing or excavating.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Redlands, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded depth near Redlands is 22 feet, and the middle half runs from 16 to 40 feet. The records are not uniform: 79% are under 100 feet, while the deepest recorded well is 1,690 feet. Many records are monitoring wells, so a household well on a particular lot may be substantially deeper.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Redlands?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $75 per foot in mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 22-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $1,100 to $1,600. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $7,100 to $13,600. Access, depth and equipment can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Redlands wells produce?
faq.a: Of the 56 records reporting yield, the median is 12.2 gallons per minute and the middle half is 7.9 to 15.0 gallons per minute. The reported results show 54% between 5 and 15 gallons per minute and 45% above 15 gallons per minute. These figures do not guarantee the yield of an untested well on a property.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Redlands?
faq.a: Permit records cannot prove that water is safe to drink. Test the well serving the property for appropriate contaminants and review nearby environmental information. Within about ten miles, the mapped records include 69 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1 historic mine feature and 13 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Treatment decisions should follow laboratory results.

faq.q: What should I check before buying land with a well in Redlands?
faq.a: Review the permit, completion report, legal use, measured depth, static level, pump yield, water test and septic layout. Only 68 records report static water level and 56 report yield, so ask for property-specific testing. Colorado DWR rules apply, and an augmentation plan may be needed in an over-appropriated basin.
